newsitem.title: UK: Czechs pledge wage, budget cuts to beat deficits.
newsitem.headline: Czechs pledge wage, budget cuts to beat deficits.

text.p: The Czech Republic, struggling with mounting trade and curent account deficits, will unveil measures to cut public sector real wages and slash budget spening this week, a senior official said on Sunday.
Pavel Stepanek, director general of the finance ministry's policy department, said the government had decided to implement "robust" steps to restore external balances by targeting domestic demand.

Severe cuts in budget spending and changes in wage policy would be among the steps to be discussed at a cabinet session on Wednesday, he said during a country presentation at the annual meeting of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD).
"We propose, for instance, that real wages in the public sector decline in real terms in 1997 compared to 1996," he said.
Stepanek declined to give more details or say how deep the budget cuts would be. However, the cuts would be across all areas except those protected by law, such as pensions.
"We expect that these measures that will be approved by the government possibly this week, will restore a more sound macroeconomic environment, especially in the area of external balance," he said.

The Czech Republic has enjoyed several years of consumption-led growth. However, this has also helped to fuel a trade deficit, which grew to 160.3 billion Czech crowns last year from 95.2 billion in 1995, and a current account deficit of 8.6 percent of gross domestic product.
There have also been signs of growth slowing or, in the industrial sector, of output declining. At the same time, real wages have soared, rising 11.4 percent year-on-year in February.
Stepanek said state representatives in part-privatised industries would also seek to influence wage policy there.
Finance Minister Ivan Kocarnik told Czech Television on Sunday the measures would only slow the growth of wages, not reduce them.

Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus, who has complained that excessively tight central bank policy has dampened growth, said on Saturday the government and bank had discussed a rate cut to kick-start the economy.
Kocarnik said the measures to be discussed this week would include an easing of monetary policy.

However, central bank board member Jan Vit told Reuters no rate changes were planned for this week after last week's cut of two percentage points in banks' minimum reserve requirements to 9.5 percent from May 8.
"To continue with an unchanged policy would be in effect implementation of a more restrictive policy," Vit said, adding the measure had been possible because of falls in money supply and inflation.
The tight policy and high rates have kept the crown strong, relative to its dollar/mark basket, but officials have repeatedly ruled out a devaluation.
Stepanek said the government expected inflation of 7.7 percent this year, after 8.8 percent in 1996 and that the government package would ensure a balanced budget.
In the medium term, he expected closer convergence with the economies of the European Union, of which the Czech republic is expected to be among the first new members from the East.
Growth was expected to average 4-5 percent a year and inflation should fall by about one percentage point a year until the economy reached EU levels by the middle of next decade.
